messages.subject: Loopy madness - Skipping To Every Third Column?
parts:
Hey All,
It's a long shot but maybe someone else has had this issue before. I'm making a nested for loop to condense a large dataframe. For each primary trapping occasion, I have three secondary trapping occasions (i.e. each month I trap for three days). Since RMark doesn't support a goodness of fit test for the Robust Design (i.e. testing all months and all days), the developers suggest simplifying the data to a form that can be tested for fit. To do this I would create a new data frame with only one column for each primary trapping occasion (i.e. month only) and just record whether a mouse was caught during any day that month or not. So what I am doing is checking if any of the three columns have a capture or not, then recording that in a new column (there is also a notation for mice in sites that werent trapped that month but I can skip over that for now, I get the same problem if I ignore it). The actual ifelse test stuff is more complex, but even with this simplified version I get the same problem which is that the for loop runs, but only every third column in the resulting data frame is filled in (i.e. only every third month is evaluated, every third i). This seems to be coincidental to the fact that I am testing three consecutive days because I tried changing that around and still every third column was skipped. I also got the error "new columns would leave holes after existing columns" sometimes, depending on how I moved stuff around. Anyway, its a weird situation and hard to describe, but maybe someone has dealt with this before and will recognize whats up. Also, I know for loops are shit so if someone has a suggestion on how to do it better I am open to that.

Thanks,
Katie



for (i in firstDates) {
  for (j in allMice) {
    nRow <- as.numeric(which(allSites.temp$MOUSEID == j))
    Date <-as.character(as.Date(i, origin = "1970-01-01"))
    nCol <- as.numeric(which(colnames(allSites.temp) == Date))
    first <- allSites.temp[nRow, nCol]      # whether the mouse was caught on the first day (1 if yes, 0 if no)
    second <- allSites.temp[nRow, nCol+1] # whether the mouse was caught on the second day
    third <- allSites.temp[nRow, nCol+2] #etc.
    stat <- ifelse((as.numeric(first))+ (as.numeric(second))+ (as.numeric(third))   ==  0, 0, 1)
    CJS[nRow,nCol] <- stat
}
}



--

parts:
Without an example my intuition is to collapse from wide format to long
format, then summarize by counting hits (using sqdlf or dplyr to get SQL
like behavior). No direct looping, only implied by the functions.

In SQL speak it's,
SELECT Count(Primary) FROM table GROUP BY Primary

This assumes you've shifted your data to look like:
Primary, Secondary, Catch
Month 1, Day 1, 1
Month 1, Day 2, 0
Month 1, Day 3, 1
Month 2...

Result would be
Primary, Count(Primary)
Month 1, 2
Month 2...
PS: You could also SUM instead of counting.

Enjoy,
Alex Mandel, PhD

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Loopy madness - Skipping To Every Third Column?
parts:
Hi Katie!

Firstly, I love for loops. I will die on this hill. Sometimes they are the clearest way to implement something. Sometimes they take way less time to try to implement than working up a solution in dplyr, using apply, etc. If anyone tries to shame you for using for loops, I will happily give them stink eye. (side note to D-RUG group at large— that offer goes for all of you).

I *think* the issue might be in storing the ‘stat’ variable to the CJS dataframe. Using ‘nRow’ to put the ‘stat’ in the proper row should be fine (since I’m guessing it corresponds to the same mouse ID number in both allSites.temp and in CJS). Using ‘nCol’ will be problematic. I think either:

1. CJS has the exact same dimensions as allSites.temp (same number of rows and number of columns), in which case the nCol variable is only ever referring to every third column (because, as you implement earlier in the looping block, nCol + 1 is what refers to the second column in each set of trapping days and nCol + 2 is what refers to the third column in each set of trapping days).

2. CJS has 1/3 fewer columns than allSites.temp, and the nCol variable is only ever going to be in multiples of 3.

You can fix this in the for loop by specifying which column of CJS you want to put `stat` using indexing based on the CJS data frame instead of the allSites.temp dataframe (which is what you currently do, by using the nCol variable)

Your for loop would look like this (changed or added lines in bold):

for (i in firstDates) { 
  for (j in allMice) { 
    nRow <- as.numeric(which(allSites.temp$MOUSEID == j))
    Date <-as.character(as.Date(i, origin = "1970-01-01"))
    nCol <- as.numeric(which(colnames(allSites.temp) == Date))
    first <- allSites.temp[nRow, nCol]      # whether the mouse was caught on the first day (1 if yes, 0 if no)
    second <- allSites.temp[nRow, nCol+1] # whether the mouse was caught on the second day 
    third <- allSites.temp[nRow, nCol+2] #etc.
    stat <- ifelse((as.numeric(first))+ (as.numeric(second))+ (as.numeric(third))   ==  0, 0, 1)

nCol_for_final_dataframe <- which(colnames(CJS) == Date)

    CJS[nRow, nCol_for_final_dataframe] <- stat
  }
}


### If you want to work with dplyr, here’s how I would do it. This is the same as Alex’s suggestion, which is a good one.

First, I make up some data in the format that is similar to what you have (based on my understanding of your for loop). Let us know if this isn’t quite right!

# Something like this?

nMice <- 5
probFound <- 0.2 # combination of detection probability and whether mouse is present
allSites.temp <- data.frame(MOUSEID = 1:nMice, month1_day1 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound), month1_day2 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound), month1_day2 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound), 
                     month2_day1 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound), month2_day2 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound), month2_day3 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound),
                     month3_day1 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound), month3_day2 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound), month3_day3 = rbinom(nMice, 1, prob = probFound))

colnames(allSites.temp) <- c("MOUSEID", 
                      "2018-01-01", "2018-01-02", "2018-01-03",
                      "2018-02-01", "2018-02-02", "2018-02-03",
                      "2018-03-01", "2018-03-02", "2018-03-03")

# The code:

library(dplyr) # To use the mutate(), group_by(), and summarize() verbs
library(tidyr) # To use gather() for converting from wide format to long format
library(lubridate) # To work more easily with date times

allSites.temp %>% 
  gather(key = trapping_date, value = trapped_or_not, -MOUSEID) %>% 
  mutate(trapping_date = ymd(trapping_date)) %>% 
  group_by(MOUSEID, trapping_month = month(trapping_date)) %>% 
  summarize(caught_in_those_three_days = any(trapped_or_not))

# The explanation:

# First, we use gather() from the tidyr package to turn the wide format to long format. To use gather(), specify a `key` (what do the column names that you are gathering represent? In this case, trapping dates), and a `value` (what do the cells in the columns to be gathered represent? In this case, whether a mouse was captured or not). We also use the minus sign for the MOUSEID column to say "I want to gather all the columns except for the ones I list with a minus sign"
# Then, I turn the trapping_date character column into a date column using the ymd() function from lubridate (ymd stands for 'year', 'month', 'day', as you might have guessed). You did this using as.Date(), which also works!
# Then I want to group the resulting data frame by MOUSEID and by trapping month. I use the month() function from lubridate to pull out the 'month' of each of the trapping efforts. There should be 3 observations per month. If you ever had a 3 day trapping period that crossed months (last day of the month, then the first 2 days of the next month, for instance), then we'd have to modify this a bit.
# We want to summarize the 3 observations into a single number (by asking: was this mouse captured at all in those three days for this trapping period?) We can use the any() function for this if your "trapped or not" observations are recorded as 0's and 1's or as FALSE's and TRUE's. If they aren't recorded this way, we can work around this. The any() function returns TRUE if any of those 3 observations were TRUE (or can be coerced to TRUE, like a 1) and FALSE otherwise (all three observations are FALSE or coerced to FALSE, like 0's)

# We want to summarize the 3 observations into a single number (by asking: was this mouse captured at all in those three days for this trapping period?) We can use the any() function for this if your "trapped or not" observations are recorded as 0's and 1's or as FALSE's and TRUE's. If they aren't recorded this way, we can work around this. The any() function returns TRUE if any of those 3 observations were TRUE (or can be coerced to TRUE, like a 1) and FALSE otherwise (all three observations are FALSE or coerced to FALSE, like 0's)

Without an example my intuition is to collapse from wide format to long
format, then summarize by counting hits (using sqdlf or dplyr to get SQL
like behavior). No direct looping, only implied by the functions.

In SQL speak it's,
SELECT Count(Primary) FROM table GROUP BY Primary

This assumes you've shifted your data to look like:
Primary, Secondary, Catch
Month 1, Day 1, 1
Month 1, Day 2, 0
Month 1, Day 3, 1
Month 2...

Result would be
Primary, Count(Primary)
Month 1, 2
Month 2...
PS: You could also SUM instead of counting.
